title: Extension of the infinitesimal Steinberg module from the Borel thickening
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], of prime characteristic $p>0$, and let $S$ be a semisimple simply connected $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Semisimple means smooth, affine, connected and of finite type, with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, where solvable means that the successive commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. Simply connected means that every surjective homomorphism $S'\to S$ from a semisimple group scheme with finite central kernel is an isomorphism; finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra and central means commuting with every element after every scalar extension. A split torus is a group scheme isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r\ge0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$; a maximal torus is one not contained in a larger torus. A Borel subgroup is a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup. Fix a split maximal torus $T\subseteq S$ and a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq T$. For this pair, let $\Phi^+$ be the positive roots given by the nonzero characters of the adjoint action of $T$ on $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$, where $\operatorname{Lie}(B)$ is the kernel of $B(F[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2))\to B(F)$, with its tangent-space structure. A character is a group-scheme homomorphism $T\to\mathbf G_m$; addition of characters means multiplication of their values. Let $\rho\in X^*(T)$ satisfy $2\rho=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$, and let $\widetilde\rho:B\to\mathbf G_m$ extend it and be trivial on the unipotent radical of $B$; this radical is its largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup, with unipotent meaning that all geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful linear representation. Fix an integer $r\ge1$ and write $q=p^r$ and $\lambda=(q-1)\rho$. If $C=F[S]$, define $S^{(q)}=\operatorname{Spec}(C\otimes_{F,a\mapsto a^q}F)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]; its group operations are obtained by this base change. The relative Frobenius $F^r_{S/F}:S\to S^{(q)}$ has coordinate map $c\otimes a\mapsto ac^q$. Let $T^{(q)}\subseteq S^{(q)}$ be the base change of $T$, let $S_r=\ker F^r_{S/F}$, and define the closed subgroup schemes $L_r=(F^r_{S/F})^{-1}(T^{(q)})$ and $P_r=B\cap L_r$, with scheme-theoretic inverse image and intersection. Use the notation $S_rT=L_r$ and $B_rT=P_r$. Let $B^{(q)}$ be the base change of $B$ and put $H_r=(F^r_{S/F})^{-1}(B^{(q)})$. Define
$$V_r=\{f\in F[H_r]:f(hb)=\widetilde\rho(b)^{q-1}f(h)\text{ for every commutative }F\text{-algebra }D,\ h\in H_r(D),\ b\in B(D)\}.$$
With its left-translation action $(a f)(h)=f(a^{-1}h)$, $V_r$ is a finite-dimensional rational $H_r$-module. There exists a rational $S$-module structure on this same $F$-vector space whose restriction to $H_r$ is this specified action. Rational means a coassociative counital $F$-linear coaction $V_r\to V_r\otimes_F F[S]$; the restriction equality is equality of coactions after the coordinate map $F[S]\to F[H_r]$, not merely equality on $F$-points. This holds for every $r\ge1$, every prime $p$ including $2$, and the trivial group. No identification with global sections on $S/B$ is asserted.

source.place: Section 2.5, equations (4)--(9), printed pp.322--323, especially (9): the module induced from B to G_rB at the Steinberg weight admits a G-module structure, citing Jantzen II.3.18. The roots in Kaneda Lie(B) are negative, whereas this statement makes them positive; its inducing character is -(q-1)rho, so the semi-invariant functions have the displayed positive covariance. Local paper WANTED; read online. This is the pre-Kempf extension input, not Jantzen II.8.8 or II.8.19.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], $S$ is reductive. By [lem-sfb-rho-regular-weyl-orbit], $\langle\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=1$ for each simple root, so $\lambda=(q-1)\rho$ is dominant. Apply [lem-sfb-integral-specialization-highest-weight-dimension] to $\eta=\lambda$ and its specified extension $\widetilde\rho^{q-1}$, obtaining a rational $S$-module $W$ and $v\ne0$ with $bv=\widetilde\rho(b)^{q-1}v$. Write $N=|\Phi^+|$. In its dimension formula $\lambda+\rho=q\rho$, so each fraction is $q$ in $\mathbf Q$ and $\dim_F W=q^N$. This uses an integral-specialization module and no dimension formula for global induced modules.

Primary PDF read online at https://msp.org/pjm/1994/163-2/pjm-v163-n2-p07-s.pdf; local copy WANTED.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-frobenius-borel-induction-geometry] to $\chi=\widetilde\rho^{-(q-1)}$. It gives an $L_r$-equivariant restriction isomorphism $V_r\simeq Z_r(\lambda)$ with exactly the covariance of the question. By [lem-sfb-frobenius-kernel-induced-dual-pbw], $Z_r(\lambda)$ is rational of dimension $q^N$; by [lem-sfb-steinberg-infinitesimal-induced-simple], it is nonzero and simple as an $L_r$-module. Therefore $V_r$ has dimension $q^N$ and is simple on restriction to $L_r$.

proof.text:
Put $W^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_F(W,F)$ with contragredient action $(a\ell)(w)=\ell(a^{-1}w)$. In a basis its action matrix is the inverse transpose of the regular action matrix on $W$, hence it is a rational $S$-action. Define $\phi:W^\vee\to V_r$ by $\phi(\ell)(h)=\ell(hv)$. This is a regular function, being a matrix coefficient of $W$ restricted to $H_r$. For every test algebra $D$, $h\in H_r(D)$ and $b\in B(D)$, one has $\ell(hbv)=\widetilde\rho(b)^{q-1}\ell(hv)$, which proves the required covariance. For $a,h\in H_r(D)$,
$$\phi(a\ell)(h)=\ell(a^{-1}hv)=\phi(\ell)(a^{-1}h)=(a\phi(\ell))(h).$$
Thus $\phi$ is linear and $H_r$-equivariant as a coaction identity.

proof.text:
Choose $\ell$ with $\ell(v)=1$. Then $\phi(\ell)(1)=1$, so the image is nonzero. Step 3 makes the image an $H_r$-submodule and hence an $L_r$-submodule. Simplicity from step 2 makes $\phi$ surjective. Both spaces have dimension $q^N$ by steps 1--2, so $\phi$ is bijective. Let $c_{W^\vee}$ be the rational $S$-coaction. Define on the specified vector space $V_r$
$$c_V=(\phi\otimes1)c_{W^\vee}\phi^{-1}.$$
Coassociativity and the counit identity follow by cancelling $\phi^{-1}\phi$ in these two identities for $c_{W^\vee}$. After $F[S]\to F[H_r]$, step 3 identifies this with the original left-translation coaction. This proves the specified restriction equality. If $S=1$, $N=0$ and all maps are between one-dimensional spaces; the argument works unchanged. All dimension calculations were in $\mathbf Z$ or $\mathbf Q$, so no division by a possibly zero element of $F$ occurs, including when $p=2$.

The item statement is unchanged and true. Step 1: semisimple implies reductive (pair node); <rho,alpha^vee>=1 for simple roots (rho-regular node), so lambda=(q-1)rho is dominant; the new node gives W of dimension q^N, each factor <q rho,alpha^vee>/<rho,alpha^vee> being q. Step 2: the induction-geometry node with chi=rho~^{-(q-1)} matches the covariance of V_r exactly; Z_r(lambda) has dimension q^N by the PBW node and is a simple L_r-module by the simplicity node, with the same L_r and P_r. Step 3: phi(l)(h)=l(hv) is a regular matrix coefficient; covariance and H_r-equivariance hold over every test algebra.
